did_you_know.text: The Jordan River marked the natural boundary in front of Canaan; here the camp waited on its bank just before entering the land.
The instructed distance — two thousand cubits — is significant: a cubit is about 45 cm, so the distance is roughly 900 meters, underscoring the sacred separation and caution around the ark.
The ark wasn’t just a ritual object; it went at the head of the camp like a military banner, signaling that the leading force was a divine presence, not merely a human strategy.
Calling the ark 'Lord of all the earth' emphasizes the idea that God rules the land itself — a claim of sovereignty that goes beyond the borders the Israelites are about to cross.
The focus on 'the soles of the priests' feet' shows the crossing is tied to the priests’ action: their stepping is presented as the turning point in the narrative, not merely a natural event.

The text notes the Jordan was 'full on all its banks' at harvest — a time when the river runs strong; crossing under such conditions was dangerous, which makes the sense of divine intervention more striking.
